title: Frontdoor velocity claims and proofmap
content:
Objective:

Quick, testable set of hero + subhead variants and a supporting proofmap to validate a frontdoor position built around predictable inference economics and operational velocity. This doc organizes copy into distinct audience paths, maps each claim to a short proof artifact, and proposes a lightweight A/B test matrix for the next sprint.

Why "frontdoor velocity"?
- We often default to latency/cost framing. That remains true, but customers buy outcomes: how fast they can ship and iterate with predictable costs and reliability. "Frontdoor velocity" ties product benefits to developer velocity and product velocity rather than just per-token economics.

Primary audiences and prioritized hooks:
1) Developers (individual/PLG): speed to prototype + low friction onboarding.
2) Platform/Infra teams: predictable SLAs, capacity controls, private deployment options.
3) Product/PMs at scale-ups: consistent UX, safe rollouts, cost predictability.

Hero copy variants (short, testable):
- Variant A (Developer-first): "Ship LLM features with server-grade predictability"
  - Subhead: "From prototype to production: predictable latency, transparent cost, same API."
- Variant B (Velocity-first): "Inference that moves as fast as your product"
  - Subhead: "Autoscaling, smart fallbacks, and per-route economics—so your team ships faster."
- Variant C (Safety + Enterprise): "Enterprise-grade inference without rebuilding the stack"
  - Subhead: "Private deployments, KMS integrations, and SLAs for regulated workloads."
- Variant D (Economics-first, but new phrasing): "Control inference economics, keep product momentum"
  - Subhead: "Guided batching, caching, and model profiles that lower unit cost—and maintain quality."

Microcopy for CTAs and scaffolding (short options to swap into pages):
- CTA primary: "Try the API" / "Start for free" / "Reserve dedicated capacity"
- Secondary CTAs: "See latency benchmarks" / "Compare deployment options" / "Request an enterprise demo"

Proofmap: mapping claims to short, linkable evidence (for engineers and GTM). The idea is each page claim links to an artifact customers and sales can trust.
- Claim: "Predictable latency at scale" -> Proof: p99 latency dashboard snapshot + SLA language + short explainer of routing logic (link to observability dashboard snippet).
- Claim: "Lower unit cost without quality loss" -> Proof: before/after evals showing same eval prompts with quantized model + cost delta table + suggested quantization profiles.
- Claim: "Flexible deployment modes" -> Proof: one-pager on Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private with architecture diagrams and a short checklist for compliance controls.
- Claim: "Safe rollouts and fallbacks" -> Proof: rollout config example (canary + automatic fallback), incident playbook excerpt, and a recorded demo.
- Claim: "Developer-friendly API" -> Proof: 3-minute quickstart video, SDK snippets, and sample app repo link.

Competitive angle (concise):
- Opponent group A: Big cloud AI endpoints — they give model access but not predictable economics and fine-grained deployment control. Position: emphasize controls and observability for unit economics.
- Opponent group B: Self-hosted/inference stacks — they deliver control but require heavy ops. Position: highlight fast onboarding and managed operational components (routing, kernels, cache) without losing deploy control for enterprises.
- Opponent group C: Simple LLM APIs — they focus on convenience; claim advantage by offering the same convenience plus observability and predictable costs at scale.

Risk notes (what reviewers will push back on):
- "Predictable" is a high bar — we must be explicit about what is covered (per-route p99 SLOs, billing smoothing/commit tiers) and what isn’t (extreme tail cases when customers supply very long sequences).
- Any cost claim needs clear context and a link to methodology. A/B test datasets must be reproducible.

Experiment matrix (weeks 0–4):
- Test 1: Hero variant A vs B on the main landing page, target: developer traffic from docs. KPI: signup conversion (30-day free credits used), secondary: docs click-through.
- Test 2: Variant C on enterprise demo flow vs control; KPI: demo requests from enterprise leads.
- Test 3: Microcopy CTA test "Try the API" vs "Start for free" among trial funnel; KPI: account creation rate.
- Test 4: Proofmap links visible vs collapsed on homepage (two experiences). KPI: time-to-click to benchmarks and demo requests.

Content & measurement definitions:
- Signup conversion: new accounts that hit the first paid or trial usage event within 7 days.
- Demo request: form submissions flagged as "enterprise" or meeting threshold metadata (company size or intended spend).
- Engagement with proof artifacts: clicks to dashboard, repo, or benchmark pages per session.

Page scaffolding recommendations (short):
- Above the fold: one hero line (A/B), one-line subhead, primary CTA, small trust strip (SLA/regions/teams using Redwood).
- Mid-page: three grouped proof cards mapping to the proofmap (Latency, Cost, Deployments). Each card has 20–40 words and a link to the artifact.
- Lower funnel: short comparison grid (hosted vs dedicated vs private) + quick FAQ about compliance and pricing anchors.

Assets to prepare before launch:
- p99 latency dashboard exports for the last 30 days (hosted+deds) with margin notes.
- Cost/eval package (scripted eval prompts, model versions, quantization settings, cost per 1k tokens).
- 2 short walkthrough videos: onboarding (3m) and canary-rollout demo (3m).
- One-page private deployment checklist for sales.

Next steps (owners & timeline):
- Week 1: Copy variants implemented on staging + linkable proof artifacts collected (Owner: Priya).
- Week 2: Run A/B tests, QA proof links, prepare analytics events (Owner: Ethan).
- Week 3: Evaluate initial signals, iterate top-performing hero + CTA (Owner: María).
- Week 4: Decide roll-out to production or iterate again based on results; capture learnings in Confluence (Owner: Priya).

Open questions for leadership / feedback needed:
- Which single proof artifact is highest priority to make truly public (SLA snippet vs latency dashboard vs cost eval)?
- Are we comfortable with the phrase "predictable" on the homepage, or do we need to qualify it more explicitly?
- What level of pricing transparency do we want on the product page vs in gated materials?

Notes to reviewers: this is intentionally compact and experiment-oriented. The goal is to trade initial polish for rapid learnings—swap hero lines and proof visibility, measure, and iterate. If you want a fully copy-edited final page, I can expand the winning variant into a complete page comp for design.
